# Asking what causes what, and drawing curves {#sec-causal-inference-splines}















At the end of @sec-linear-regression-multiple I left a loose end in plain sight. GFAP, the marker of reactive astrocytes, goes up after an ischemia; tissue area goes down; the two travel together across the animals. And yet, once the day after the lesion was in the model, the GFAP coefficient shrank to about zero and I wrote that GFAP "carries no additional predictive information beyond time". I was careful to say *predictive*. I was also careful to say that I was not claiming that GFAP "has no effect" on tissue area, and that the causal diagrams would come later. This is the chapter where they come.

The question that I think every bench scientist has asked of a marker is the one in the title of this section: **does GFAP drive the loss of tissue, or does it just move with it?** Those are two different questions, and the data of @sec-linear-regression-multiple cannot tell them apart, because a regression only ever answers the second one. @fig-cis_hook is that old problem, drawn with all 49 animals and all five days (the earlier chapter used three of them).






::: {.cell}

In the left panel of @fig-cis_hook, the dashed line goes down: across all 49 animals, GFAP and tissue area have a correlation of -0.29, and the slope is -0.34 mm² per 100 units of GFAP. In the right panel, each colored line compares animals that share a day, and these lines are nearly flat; the slope that pools them (the model with the day in it) is 0.1 mm² per 100 units. The same variable, the same animals and the opposite sign, depending on what you hold fixed. A regression coefficient cannot say which of the two is the answer to *your* question, because the two answers come from different comparisons, and which comparison is the right one depends on how the variables are connected in the animal. That connection is not in the data file. It is in your head, in the literature and in the design of the experiment, and a [causal diagram]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} is simply a way of writing it down so that a colleague (or a reviewer) can argue with it.

This chapter has two halves that look unrelated and are not. The first is about **causes**: a small vocabulary of arrows that tells you what to adjust for and, more important, what *not* to adjust for. The second is about **curves**: the spline, a flexible line that lets the adjustment, and sometimes the relationship you care about, bend as far as the tissue does. They share a chapter because each one repairs a limit of the other. A diagram tells you *which* variables belong in the model; a spline lets them enter in the shape they really have, instead of the straight line that I have been forcing on them since @sec-linear-regression-what. The question they answer together is: what does *X* do to *Y*, once I have accounted for what else is going on, without squeezing a curve into a line?

## Three shapes: the lamp, the water and the pond {#sec-cis-shapes}

Every causal diagram, however large, is built from three small shapes, and each one is easiest to understand as a scene before it is a diagram (@fig-cis_sketch).

![One lamp lighting two windows (a fork), water running through two tanks (a pipe), and two streams meeting in a pond where the fish you catch depend on both (a collider).](images/causal-inference-splines_three-shapes.png){#fig-cis_sketch fig-align="center" width="95%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch in three panels separated by thin vertical lines. Left: one street lamp between two cottages, with a lit window in each. Middle: a round glass tank on a stone base sending water through a pipe into a second glass tank. Right: a teal stream and an ochre stream running into the same pond, with a small seated fisher on a rock holding a rod over the water."}

Picture a lamp on a pole between two houses, lighting a window in each. If you stand in the street and watch the two windows, they come on and go off together, and an observer who has not seen the lamp could swear that one window is switching the other. Neither is. They share a **common cause**. That shape is a [fork]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: the lamp (*Z*) points to both windows (*X* and *Y*). The two windows are correlated *only because of the lamp*, and the correlation vanishes once you hold the lamp fixed: among the evenings when the lamp is on, the windows have nothing more to say to each other.

Now picture two tanks joined by a pipe. You fill the top one (*X*), the water runs through the pipe into the middle tank (*Z*), and from there into the bottom one (*Y*). If you want to know what filling the top tank does to the bottom one, you must *not* close the middle valve: holding *Z* fixed would stop the very water you are trying to follow. That shape is a [pipe]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: *X* acts on *Y through* *Z*, and *Z* is a **mediator**. A pipe and a fork are statistically twins (both make *X* and *Y* correlated, and both make them independent once *Z* is held fixed) but they ask for opposite treatment, and that is the first warning of the chapter: the data cannot tell you which one you have.

The third shape is the one that surprised me when I first met it. Two streams, one from the north and one from the south, run into the same pond. The streams have nothing to do with each other. But suppose you only count the *fish you catch*, and suppose you only catch a fish when the pond is good for it, which happens when the northern water is clean, or the southern water is, or both. Among the fish you caught, the two streams now look related: if the northern water was poor, the southern water must have been good, or you would not have had a fish. That shape is a [collider]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: two causes (*X* and *Y*) meet in a common effect (*Z*), and the harm comes from *conditioning on that effect*, by selecting on it, or holding it fixed, or including it in a model. A fork is repaired by holding *Z* fixed; a pipe is broken by it; a collider is *created* by it.

The books give each shape a favorite example. @mcelreath2020 uses the correlation between the number of Waffle House restaurants and the divorce rate across US states for the fork, a soil treatment that reduces a fungus and so helps plants grow for the pipe, and funded grant proposals, in which rigor and novelty look negatively correlated only because a panel funds a proposal that has at least one of them, for the collider. @huntingtonklein2021 has the colleague who orders sandwiches after you have bought your own: among the people who end up eating a sandwich, not having bought one means that you were given one. And @gelman2020 give the home-visit program that improves parenting and so raises a child's IQ as the pipe, in the discussion of why it is wrong to adjust for an intermediate outcome. @fig-cis_three_dags writes the three shapes with the names of the variables of this book, one for each of the data sets that I use in the chapter.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Fork: one common cause of two markers
dag_fork <- dagitty("dag { Ischemia -> GFAP; Ischemia -> PDGFRB }")
coordinates(dag_fork) <- list(x = c(Ischemia = 1, GFAP = 0, PDGFRB = 2), y = c(Ischemia = 1, GFAP = 0, PDGFRB = 0))
p_fork <- plot_dag(dag_fork, labels = c(Ischemia = "Ischemia", GFAP = "GFAP", PDGFRB = "PDGFR-β"),
                   role = c(Ischemia = "other", GFAP = "exposure", PDGFRB = "outcome"), xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3), w_in = 3.1, h_in = 2.0) +
  ggtitle("Fork") + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

# Pipe: the ischemia acts on tissue through a marker
dag_pipe <- dagitty("dag { Ischemia -> GFAP -> Area }")
coordinates(dag_pipe) <- list(x = c(Ischemia = 0, GFAP = 1, Area = 2), y = c(Ischemia = 0, GFAP = 0, Area = 0))
p_pipe <- plot_dag(dag_pipe, labels = c(Ischemia = "Ischemia", GFAP = "GFAP", Area = "Tissue\narea"),
                   role = c(Ischemia = "exposure", GFAP = "other", Area = "outcome"), xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.7, 0.7), w_in = 3.1, h_in = 2.0) +
  ggtitle("Pipe") + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

# Collider: genotype and strength both decide whether the attempt is completed
dag_coll <- dagitty("dag { Genotype -> Completed <- Strength }")
coordinates(dag_coll) <- list(x = c(Genotype = 0, Strength = 2, Completed = 1), y = c(Genotype = 1, Strength = 1, Completed = 0))
p_coll <- plot_dag(dag_coll, labels = c(Genotype = "Genotype", Strength = "Strength", Completed = "Completed\nthe crossing"),
                   role = c(Genotype = "exposure", Strength = "outcome", Completed = "other"), xlim = c(-0.6, 2.6), ylim = c(-0.5, 1.3), w_in = 3.1, h_in = 2.0) +
  ggtitle("Collider") + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

p_fork + p_pipe + p_coll
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
A causal diagram is a map of claims, and each arrow says "this one acts on that one". Read it in three steps. First, find the arrows into the variable you care about as an outcome: those are the things the diagram says can move it. Second, find every route that connects the exposure and the outcome, going *against* the arrows too (the fork connects the two markers through the ischemia even though no arrow joins them). Third, ask of each route whether it carries a *cause* (it follows the arrows from the exposure to the outcome) or only an *association* (it goes through a common cause or through a variable that two arrows point into), and whether holding some variable fixed would open or close it. The mistake to avoid is to read the diagram as a result. It is not. It is what you are willing to *assume*, drawn so that somebody can disagree with it.
:::

I drew @fig-cis_three_dags with `dagitty` [@textor2016] (to hold the graph) and `ggdag` [@ggdag] (to turn it into coordinates), and then with plain `ggplot2` (boxes and arrows), instead of the default plot of either package, for two reasons. The graph is an object that `dagitty` can *query*, as you will see in a moment, so the picture and the logic come from one source. And a static `ggplot` renders identically in the web edition and in the PDF, which the interactive alternatives do not. The design tip to take away is the one that every diagram in this chapter follows: color the exposure and the outcome, draw an uncertain arrow dashed, and draw a variable you never measured in grey. A reader should be able to see the *claims* of the graph before reading a word of the caption.

### What each shape asks you to do {#sec-cis-shapes-do}

I will tie the three shapes to the data of the book, because the first time I saw them in the abstract I nodded and forgot them. The **fork** is already in this book, under another name. GFAP and PDGFR-β are correlated across the animals (0.52), and a reader of @sec-eda-ggpairs would call them "collinear". That word describes the correlation and is silent about its source. If the ischemia pushes both up, the correlation is a fork, and it is not a defect of the data that needs to be "fixed" by dropping one of them (the thread of @sec-linear-regression-assumptions): it is what the biology produces, and the only question is whether the model should hold the ischemia fixed. The **pipe** is the question of this chapter: if the ischemia reaches the tissue through GFAP, then holding GFAP fixed removes the very effect I want to measure. And the **collider** is hiding in the hanging-wire analyses of @sec-beta-robust-regression, @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes and @sec-multilevel-glmm, which kept only the attempts that were completed, and in the missing sections of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts; I come back to both.

The summary of the three shapes is one sentence each, and it is worth memorizing, because the rest of the chapter is this sentence applied:

- **Fork** (a common cause of *X* and *Y*): *X* and *Y* are associated without any arrow between them. **Hold the common cause fixed** (adjust for it) to remove the association that is not causal.
- **Pipe** (*X* acts on *Y* through *Z*): the association between *X* and *Y* is partly or wholly causal. **Do not hold *Z* fixed** if you want the total effect of *X*; do it only if you want the part of the effect that does not go through *Z*.
- **Collider** (*X* and *Y* both act on *Z*): *X* and *Y* are independent until you look at *Z*. **Do not hold *Z* fixed**, do not select on it and do not drop the rows where it is missing: that opens a route that was closed.

## Reading an adjustment set from a diagram {#sec-cis-backdoor}

Think of the effect you are after as a visitor who walks into a house by the front door. The causal path from *X* to *Y* is the front door, and it starts with an arrow that *leaves* *X*. A **[backdoor path]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}** is any other way into the house: a route from *X* to *Y* that starts with an arrow that *enters* *X* (it begins "*X* ←"). Through the back door walk the associations that are not effects: the lamp that lights both windows, the ischemia that raises both markers. To estimate the effect of *X* on *Y*, you want the front door open and every back door shut. An [adjustment set]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} is the list of variables that, when held fixed in the model, shuts the back doors *without* closing the front door and *without* opening a new one.

The procedure is mechanical, and that is its charm. List every path between *X* and *Y*, ignoring the direction of the arrows. Mark the ones that start with an arrow into *X*. Choose variables to hold fixed so that every marked path is blocked: a path through a fork or a pipe is blocked by holding its middle variable fixed; a path through a collider is blocked *unless* you hold the collider (or something it causes) fixed. And never put in the set a mediator that you want the total effect to pass through. This is the **backdoor criterion**, and the books give it with different amounts of algebra [@pearl2009; @mcelreath2020; @huntingtonklein2021]. You do not have to do it by hand: `dagitty::adjustmentSets()` does the search and is a good check on the hand version. @tbl-cis_controls is the list of the kinds of variable that you may be tempted to put in a model, and what the diagram says about each. It is the habit of the chapter in a table: **draw the diagram before you choose the covariates, and look every covariate up in it.**






::: {#tbl-cis_controls .cell tbl-cap='Kinds of variable and what a causal diagram says about putting them in the model, with a case of this book for each.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# One row per kind of variable: the shape it belongs to, the case of this book, and the advice
controls <- data.frame(
  Kind = c("Confounder (common cause of the exposure and the outcome)",
           "Mediator (on the way from the exposure to the outcome)",
           "Collider (a common effect of two causes)",
           "Descendant of a collider",
           "Descendant of the outcome",
           "Cause of the exposure only",
           "Cause of the outcome only"),
  `A case of this book` = c("Sex, in the speech of the Parkinson participants: it differs between groups and changes speech",
                            "GFAP, between the ischemia and the tissue area (if the barrier acts on the tissue)",
                            "Completing the wire crossing: it depends on genotype and on strength",
                            "Any measurement that is higher when the attempt was completed",
                            "A medication that is prescribed because of the diagnosis, when the diagnosis is the outcome of interest",
                            "The day of sacrifice, when the question is about the lesion and the days were assigned at random",
                            "Age, in a comparison of groups that are matched on age"),
  `What to do` = c("Adjust: it closes a back door.",
                   "Leave out for the total effect; put in only to ask for the part of the effect that does not go through it, and say what that needs.",
                   "Leave out, and do not select rows by it.",
                   "Leave out: it is a weak version of the collider.",
                   "Leave out: it selects on the outcome and shrinks the effect.",
                   "Optional: it closes no back door and costs precision.",
                   "Optional: it closes no back door and can buy precision."),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(controls)
```

Two rows of @tbl-cis_controls need a word, because they are the ones that I did not expect. The first is the last two: a variable that *causes only the exposure* does not close any back door (there is none through it), and it does nothing for the estimate except to take away some of the variation in the exposure that you needed. @mcelreath2020 calls it a precision parasite. A variable that *causes only the outcome* is harmless and can even help, by soaking up variation that would otherwise be noise, and that is the sense in which the age adjustment of the Parkinson example will matter or not. The second is the descendants: a variable that is caused by a collider is a noisy copy of it, and holding it fixed partly holds the collider fixed. That is why "controlling for a consequence" is risky even when the consequence is not the thing that two causes meet in.

Here are three tiny graphs, one for each shape, and what `dagitty` says. The point of the chunk is that the software and your intuition about the shapes should agree, and that you can ask it a question: *what must I adjust for to get the effect of the exposure on the outcome?*

adjustmentSets(dag_fork, exposure = "GFAP", outcome = "PDGFRB", effect = "total")

The output reads like this. For the fork, the first line says that to compare the two markers without the ischemia's influence, the set is the ischemia (`{ Ischemia }`). For the pipe, the total effect of the ischemia needs nothing (`{}`, the empty set: no back door exists) and the direct effect, the part that does not go through GFAP, needs GFAP (`{ GFAP }`). And for the collider, `dseparated()` answers `TRUE` for "are these two independent?" when nothing is held fixed, and `FALSE` when the crossing is: holding the collider fixed creates the association. The code is trivial and the sentence it supports is not: *which* variables belong in the model is a consequence of the graph, not of the data.

## Does GFAP drive the tissue loss? {#sec-cis-cell}

Now the question of the hook, with the experiment drawn. I asked Daniel's own account of the biology before drawing anything, because the arrows are claims about the animal and it is not for the statistician to invent them. The ischemia triggers both markers. GFAP is a reactive astrocyte protein, and those astrocytes form a barrier around the lesion that keeps the harmful substances released by the dead tissue from reaching the healthy tissue next to it: a fence around the lesion. PDGFR-β cells sit in the center of the lesion, inside the fence, and the spatial chapters of the next part will show GFAP enclosing them. That gives the arrows of @fig-cis_cell_dag. And there is a fact of the *design*, stated by Daniel, that belongs in the diagram: the assignment of the animals to sham or ischemia was random, and the day after the lesion is simply the group that each animal was assigned to at the start. So nothing points into the group node: the randomization erased the arrows that would otherwise come from the animal's own characteristics.

One more thing about the design, and it is the one that I flagged when I wrote @sec-linear-regression-multiple: the only sham animals are at day 0 and every later day is ischemia. In this data set, "ischemia or not" and "how many days after it" are *the same variable*, the group, and the diagram has one node for it, not two. What I can estimate is the difference between the average animal of a given group and the average sham animal. I cannot separate what the lesion does from what time does, and no diagram will give me back a sham group at day 14 (the empty cubbies of @sec-linear-regression-multiple, again).






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

  Group [exposure] Area [outcome] U [unobserved]
  Group -> GFAP; Group -> PDGFRB; Group -> Area
  GFAP -> Area; PDGFRB -> Area
  U -> GFAP; U -> PDGFRB; U -> Area
}")
coordinates(dag_cell_u) <- list(x = c(Group = 0, GFAP = 1.2, PDGFRB = 1.2, Area = 3, U = 2.3),
                                y = c(Group = 1, GFAP = 2, PDGFRB = 0, Area = 1, U = 3))

# The same graph without U, to compare what the diagram says about the direct effect
dag_cell <- dagitty("dag {
  Group [exposure] Area [outcome]
  Group -> GFAP; Group -> PDGFRB; Group -> Area
  GFAP -> Area; PDGFRB -> Area
}")
coordinates(dag_cell) <- list(x = c(Group = 0, GFAP = 1.2, PDGFRB = 1.2, Area = 3), y = c(Group = 1, GFAP = 2, PDGFRB = 0, Area = 1))

         labels = c(Group = "Group\n(sham at day 0,\nischemia days 3 to 30)", GFAP = "GFAP", PDGFRB = "PDGFR-β",

         dashed = c("GFAP->Area", "PDGFRB->Area"), xlim = c(-0.9, 3.7), ylim = c(-0.4, 3.4), w_in = 7.2, h_in = 4.0)

I added one variable that you will not find in the data file: the *lesion size of each animal*. The same occlusion does not damage every brain to the same extent, and an animal with a larger lesion will have more reactive GFAP, more PDGFR-β and less tissue, whatever the day. It is an unmeasured common cause, and by drawing it as a grey box I am saying out loud that the experiment does not rule it out. Whether it is *there* is a biological judgment that the reader should check; I have drawn it because I would not believe a diagram of an ischemia experiment without it.

The first answer is `{}`: **the total effect needs no adjustment**, because the group was randomized and so no back door exists. That is the whole value of the randomization, and it is the one thing in this chapter that the data do not have to be believed for. The estimate is the difference between the mean tissue area of a group and the mean of the sham group, and it is the quantity that the first model below estimates. The second answer is `{ GFAP, PDGFRB }`: if the diagram has no lesion size in it, the *direct* effect, the part of the effect of the lesion that does not travel through the markers, is estimated by holding both markers fixed. But the third answer is empty, with no set printed: with the lesion size in the graph, **the direct effect cannot be estimated from these variables, whatever we hold fixed**.

The reason is the collider that I promised. A marker is a pipe (the group acts on it) *and*, because the lesion size also acts on it, a collider on the path *Group → GFAP ← Lesion size → Area*. Holding the marker fixed, which is what you do to get the direct effect, opens that path: it makes the group and the lesion size look associated among animals that have the same GFAP, and the lesion size reaches the tissue area. @mcelreath2020 calls this a "haunted" mediator: you adjusted to remove something, and a ghost that you never measured came in through the door that you opened. The practical consequence is large and easy to forget. *The coefficient of a marker in a model that also contains the group is not the effect of the marker*, and a "direct effect" estimated by adjusting for it holds only if you are willing to say that the lesion size does not exist, or does not matter.

I fit both models, with the day-by-day spread of @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression (which is where the earlier chapter found that day 3 is much more variable than the others), a prior that says that the differences between days are within about 10 mm² (`Normal(0, 5)`) and the markers in units of their own standard deviation (313 units for GFAP and 426 for PDGFR-β), so that a coefficient is the change in mm² per standard deviation of the marker. I fit two more models, with one marker at a time, because they are the ones that make the bad control visible.

### The coefficients of the covariates are not their effects {#sec-cis-table2}

There is a habit in epidemiology that has a name, the **[Table 2 fallacy]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}** [@westreich2013]: Table 1 of a paper describes the groups and Table 2 reports a model, with the exposure and, below it, the coefficient of every variable that was adjusted for. The fallacy is to read those lower rows as effects. They are not, because the variables were chosen to remove the back doors of *one* exposure, and the back doors of *their* effects are another matter: from the point of view of the group, GFAP is a mediator, but if you ask what GFAP does, the group becomes a confounder and the lesion size a back door that the model never closed. @gelman2026 describe the same problem as a *degenerate analysis*: a model built to give the causal effect of one treatment does not give causal effects for its controls, and reporting them as if it did is misleading. McElreath's remedy is the simplest one: do not show them [@mcelreath2020]. In this chapter I show the marker coefficients once, above, so that you can see what they look like, and in the sentence for the paper (below) I do not report them.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it: the lesion and the tissue"}
**Results.** Compared with the sham animals (n = 7), the mean tissue area was 5.1 [4.1, 6.0] mm² smaller at day 14 (n = 12; posterior probability of a smaller area above 0.999) and 6.5 [5.5, 7.6] mm² smaller at day 30 (n = 11), and 2.3 [-0.1, 4.5] mm² larger at day 3 (n = 8) (differences in the mean; posterior medians and 95% credible intervals). Holding GFAP and PDGFR-β fixed changed the day-14 and day-30 differences to 4.9 [3.5, 6.2] and 6.0 [4.6, 7.4] mm² smaller; the part of the effect of the lesion that does not go through these two markers could not be separated from the effect of an unmeasured common cause, such as the size of each lesion.

**Methods.** The assignment of animals to sham or to an ischemia group was random, and the day is the group each animal was assigned to at the start, so the group was not adjusted for anything (adjustment set: the empty set, from the causal diagram in the figure). Tissue area was modeled with a Gaussian likelihood with a different spread for each day, in `brms` (priors Normal(14, 5) for the sham mean and Normal(0, 5) for the differences; four chains of 3,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 for all parameters). Sham animals exist only at day 0, so the effect of the lesion and the effect of time are not separable. The coefficients of the markers are not reported as effects.
:::

## The attempts that never made it into the table {#sec-cis-wire}













![A river with a gate that lets only some fish through: the fish you measure downstream are not a sample of the fish that started upstream.](images/causal-inference-splines_river-gate.png){#fig-cis_gate fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a river with a wooden slatted gate across it. Imagine a river with a gate across it that lets only some fish through (@fig-cis_gate). A colleague counts the fish *downstream* and compares two strains that were released upstream in equal numbers. If the gate is easier for one strain than for the other, the downstream sample is not a sample of the strains; it is a sample of the fish that *got through*, and what gets a fish through is part of what you are trying to measure. The comparison of the strains downstream is not wrong because the counting was careless. It is wrong because of what the gate selected.

The gate in this book is the sixty-second clock of the hanging-wire test. In the chapters on behavior, varying slopes and multilevel GLMs I modeled the time that a mouse took to cross the wire *among the attempts that ended in a crossing*, and in @sec-missing-data-measurement-error I confessed that this left out 51 of the 567 attempts: 42 of 315 attempts of the knockout mice and 9 of 252 of the controls, which is about 3.7 times as often. That chapter explained the problem as censoring: the missing times are the *long* ones, so what is missing depends on what is missing. The diagram gives the same problem a second name, and I find that seeing both names is what makes the problem stick.

A mouse crosses the wire in a time that depends on its genotype and on its strength, which the data do not contain and which I draw as an unmeasured variable. Whether the attempt is *completed* also depends on both: a weak mouse falls or hangs until the clock stops, and a knockout mouse, whatever its strength, is more likely to fail. The genotype was given by breeding, so it is unrelated to the strength of the animal before the test. In @fig-cis_wire the left panel draws that. The crossing time is only *observed* when the attempt is completed, so an analysis of the completed attempts holds the variable `Completed` fixed at "yes". That variable is a collider of genotype and strength.






::: {.cell}

Here is the two-names story, in order. Dropping the capped attempts compares the knockouts that *crossed* with the controls that *crossed*. Among the knockouts, the filter let through a larger share of the strong mice than among the controls, because knockouts that were weak were more likely to be stopped by the clock; so the knockouts who are left are a *better* sample of knockouts than the controls who are left are of controls. The *same* statement in the language of the previous chapter is that the censoring is **informative**: the times that are missing are missing because they are long, and long is what the genotype causes. A [collider]{.ix} and an informative censoring are not two problems. They are one problem that a causal diagram and a likelihood describe from different sides, and the repair is the same in both: stop conditioning on completion. Keep every attempt in the model, as the censored model does, or model completion itself.

### Standardization: from a regression to a causal effect {#sec-cis-standardization}

Modeling completion itself is the thing I did in @sec-logistic-regression and @sec-missing-data-measurement-error, and there I used a device without telling you its name. I fit a model for the probability of an outcome, asked it what it would predict for *every* mouse in the sample if that mouse were a knockout, asked again as if every mouse were a control, and averaged the difference. I called that the average predictive comparison [@gelman2020]. Its other name is [standardization]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (epidemiologists call it *g-computation*), and it is the bridge between a regression and a causal question. The picture to hold is a photocopier. The sample is a set of mice with their own days and attempts. You photocopy it twice, relabel every mouse in one copy as a knockout and in the other as a control, let the model predict the outcome for every row in each copy, and compare the averages. Because the two copies contain *the same mice*, they differ in nothing but the label.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The model of the chapter on missing data: not completing an attempt, with a level for each mouse
fit_w10 <- readRDS("models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit10.rds")

# Standardization, step by step: (1) the data twice, once as every mouse a knockout and once as a control
nd_ko <- attempts; nd_ko$genotype <- factor("KO", levels = c("WT", "KO"))
nd_wt <- attempts; nd_wt$genotype <- factor("WT", levels = c("WT", "KO"))

# (2) The model's predicted probability of not completing, for every attempt in each copy and every posterior draw
# (3) The average over the attempts, for each draw: the share expected if everybody were a knockout, or a control
p_ko <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(fit_w10, newdata = nd_ko))
p_wt <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(fit_w10, newdata = nd_wt))
risk_diff <- 100 * (p_ko - p_wt)
```
:::






Averaged over the attempts of the experiment, the probability of not completing an attempt is 12.3 [8.6, 17.1]% if all the mice were knockouts and 4.1 [1.9, 8.7]% if all were controls, a difference of 8.1 [0.9, 14.3] percentage points. It is a *causal* statement, and I want to be precise about when I am allowed to read it as one, because the books are. A standardized difference is a causal effect under three assumptions [@gelman2020; @huntingtonklein2021]. **Exchangeability:** once the covariates in the model are held fixed, the groups would have had the same outcome if given the same genotype, that is, no back door is open. Here the genotype is given by breeding, so the arrows into it come only from the breeding itself (the litter, the cage, which I have not modeled), and the model holds the training day fixed, which does not matter for the genotype. **Positivity:** every kind of attempt in the model could have been made by a mouse of either genotype; that is true here, since both genotypes have every day. **Consistency:** the "knockout" that I predict is the knockout that exists, with no interference between mice. None of the three is a statistical result. They are the diagram, in words, and the same procedure applied with a different diagram (say, a model that had a variable *caused by* the genotype in it) would produce a number with the same format and a very different meaning.

This is the sense of the chapter's first sentence. A regression gives you a *conditional contrast*; standardization turns it into a contrast about the population by averaging over the covariates; and the diagram says whether that contrast is the effect of the exposure or merely an association. And the collider shows what happens when the diagram says no: the same recipe, applied to the completed attempts only, would give a number for a population that no longer exists.

## A line that is allowed to bend {#sec-cis-splines}













A straight line is a decision. Every model of this book so far has made it for me: one slope, the same change in the outcome for every unit of the predictor, wherever you are on the axis. In @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous I refused to extend the line beyond day 14, in @sec-longitudinal-timeseries I drew curves from a recipe and from a Gaussian process, and the earlier chapters kept reminding you that a line is a *local* description. This section is the third way to let a line bend, and the one that I use most often at my own desk: the [spline]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}.

The word comes from the shipyard. Before computers, a naval architect who needed the curve of a hull would pin a long, thin, flexible strip of wood or metal to the drawing at a few points, hold it there with lead weights, and let the strip bend. The strip assumes the smoothest shape that is compatible with the points it is made to pass through: it does not zigzag, because bending costs energy, and it does not stay straight, because the weights pull it. A statistical spline is that strip, with the weights replaced by data (@fig-cis_strip).

![A shipbuilder's flexible strip held in place by lead weights: it takes the smoothest shape that the weights allow.](images/causal-inference-splines_shipbuilders-strip.png){#fig-cis_strip fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a drafting table with a faint ship hull profile drawn on a sheet of paper and a long thin wooden strip bending in one smooth curve across it, held at five points by small grey lead weights shaped like ducks, with a pencil, a set square, a cup of pencils and a bowl of spare weights at the edges."}

### Building blocks and weights {#sec-cis-basis}

How does a computer build a bendy line from a regression? With the machinery you already have. Divide the predictor's range into small stretches, bounded by points called [knots]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;" ix="knot"}. Over each stretch define a small hill-shaped function, a [basis function]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, that is large around its own stretch and zero far from it. Then the curve is a weighted sum of the hills: stack a few of them, each multiplied by its own number (its weight), and the sum is smooth because the hills overlap smoothly. @mcelreath2020 writes it as a linear model, $\mu_i = \alpha + w_1 B_{i,1} + w_2 B_{i,2} + \dots$, where the $B$'s are the basis functions evaluated at the $i$-th observation and the weights $w$ "act like slopes". It is just another regression, with some synthetic predictors, and that is how @gelman2020 introduce it: a spline is a linear regression whose predictors are known nonlinear functions of the input. The picture to hold is a row of friends with flashlights, each lighting a patch of the wall near them, with the weight being how brightly each shines. @fig-cis_basis builds a curve in front of you, with the speech data that we use below: the rate of speech timing (in standard deviations) against the age of each of the 130 participants.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Six cubic B-spline basis functions of age; they add up to 1 at every age
basis_age <- splines::bs(pk$age, df = 6, intercept = TRUE)
w_fit <- coef(lm(pk$z_rate ~ 0 + basis_age))

# Evaluate the basis on a fine grid of ages, and weight each function
grid_age <- seq(min(pk$age), max(pk$age), length.out = 200)
B <- predict(basis_age, newx = grid_age)
fn_lab <- paste("Function", 1:6)
long_basis <- data.frame(age = rep(grid_age, 6), fn = rep(fn_lab, each = 200), plain = as.vector(B), weighted = as.vector(sweep(B, 2, w_fit, "*")))
curve_age <- data.frame(age = grid_age, y = as.vector(B %*% w_fit))
cols6 <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#CC79A7")

# Panels A and B: the functions, plain and weighted
pa <- ggplot(long_basis, aes(x = age, y = plain, color = fn)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols6) + labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Value of the function", title = "A. Building blocks") +
  Plot_theme + legend_none() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, hjust = 0))
pb <- ggplot(long_basis, aes(x = age, y = weighted, color = fn)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols6) + labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Function times its weight", title = "B. Weighted") +
  Plot_theme + legend_none() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, hjust = 0))

# Panel C: the sum of the weighted functions over the participants
pc <- ggplot() + geom_point(data = pk, aes(x = age, y = z_rate), color = "grey50", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = curve_age, aes(x = age, y = y), linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Rate of speech timing (z)", title = "C. Their sum") +
  Plot_theme + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, hjust = 0))
pa + pb + pc
```

I drew @fig-cis_basis with `splines::bs()` and `lm()` instead of the model that I will use later, because the point is the *mechanism*, and the mechanism is visible only when the building blocks are on the page. Look at it left to right. In A, each function is a hill that matters over its own stretch of ages and is zero elsewhere. In B, each hill has been scaled by its weight, and some hills have turned upside down (negative weights). In C, the black curve is nothing but their sum, and it follows the cloud of participants without being told what shape the cloud has. Read panels A to C as one sentence. The functions in A are the vocabulary the curve is allowed to use, the weights of B are what the data said, and the curve of C is the sentence that results. Ask two questions of any spline. *How many building blocks did it use?* More blocks give a curve that can change direction more often. *How were the weights chosen?* If they were chosen only to follow the points as closely as possible, the curve will follow the noise too. Which is the next section's problem. The mistake to avoid is to read the individual weights: they are the coordinates of the curve in a particular basis, not quantities with a meaning of their own.
:::

### Why a penalty {#sec-cis-penalty}

Six blocks are a choice, and the choice is delicate. With too few, the curve cannot bend where the data bend. With too many, a least-squares fit will use all of them to chase every point. The answer of the statisticians is not to find the Goldilocks number of blocks. It is to take plenty of them, more than you need, and *penalize* the weights: a tax on wiggliness, which the fit pays only if the wiggle improves the description enough to be worth it. A good way to think of the penalty is the rubber of the shipbuilder's strip: the strip can bend as much as you like, but the more it bends, the more it costs. The tuning of the tax is the whole art, and it is a parameter of the model, the smoothing parameter, estimated from the data: by REML in `mgcv`, and in `brms` by a standard deviation on the weights.

That last sentence is the part that connects splines to the rest of this book. The Bayesian version of the penalty is the multilevel model of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts. The wiggly part of the weights is given a prior, $w_k \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_s^2)$, and the standard deviation $\sigma_s$ is a parameter that the data learn, exactly as the spread between mice is. When $\sigma_s$ is small, the weights are pulled toward zero and the curve toward a straight line; when it is large, the weights are free and the curve can wiggle. It is partial pooling again, applied to the building blocks instead of to mice: the weights of a smooth are shrunk toward each other and the amount of shrinkage is estimated [@wood2017; @brms]. The same thing is what Inchausti recommends as the sensible alternative to high-degree polynomials, which explode at the edges of the data [@inchausti2023].

@fig-cis_penalty shows the tax at three levels, for the same data and ten building blocks, using `mgcv`.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Three fits that differ only in the smoothing parameter: nearly zero, estimated by REML, and enormous
fits_pen <- list(
  "No penalty" = gam(z_rate ~ group + sex + s(age, k = 10, sp = 1e-6), data = pk),
  "Penalty chosen by REML" = gam(z_rate ~ group + sex + s(age, k = 10), data = pk, method = "REML"),
  "Very strong penalty" = gam(z_rate ~ group + sex + s(age, k = 10, sp = 1e8), data = pk)
)
grid_hc <- data.frame(age = grid_age, group = "HC", sex = "M")
pen_curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits_pen), function(n) {
  data.frame(model = paste0(n, " (", round(summary(fits_pen[[n]])$s.table[1, 1], 1), ")"), age = grid_age,
             y = as.vector(predict(fits_pen[[n]], grid_hc, type = "terms", terms = "s(age)")))
}))
pen_curves$model <- factor(pen_curves$model, levels = unique(pen_curves$model))

# Points: the age part of the fit plus what is left over, from the fit with the penalty chosen by the data
g_reml <- fits_pen[["Penalty chosen by REML"]]
pk$partial_age <- as.vector(predict(g_reml, type = "terms", terms = "s(age)") + residuals(g_reml, type = "working"))

# One panel per level of the penalty
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = pk, aes(x = age, y = partial_age), color = "grey50", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = pen_curves, aes(x = age, y = y), linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Age effect on the rate (z)") +
  Plot_theme + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"))
```

### Priors for a smooth: curves, not coefficients {#sec-cis-spline-priors}

In `brms` a smooth is written `s(age10)`, with the same syntax as `mgcv`, and the fit is the multilevel model of the previous paragraph: a slope for the straight part of the curve (an ordinary coefficient, with the prior of the other coefficients), and a set of penalized weights for the bending part, with the standard deviation `sds` as the tax. The prior that matters is the one on `sds`, and the lesson of @sec-longitudinal-timeseries applies unchanged: a prior on a curve is a prior on *curves*, and the way to choose it is to draw them. I put `Normal(0, 1)` on the intercept and the coefficients, `Exponential(1)` on `sigma` and `Exponential(1)` on `sds`, all on the scale of the outcome in standard deviations, and draw the curves that this prior proposes before it has seen the data (@fig-cis_prior_curves).






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Priors on the standardized outcome: coefficients of about one standard deviation, and the same for the smooth
pr_pk <- c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
           prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma"), prior(exponential(1), class = "sds"))

# Prior-only fit: sample_prior = "only" ignores the likelihood, so the draws are curves from the prior alone
fit_p_prior <- brm(
  z_rate ~ group + sex + s(age10, k = 6),
  data = pk, prior = pr_pk, sample_prior = "only",
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/causal-inference-splines_fit5.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```

### The frequentist counterpart, and when to prefer each curve {#sec-cis-splines-which}

The frequentist spline is the same object. `mgcv::gam()` fits it with the penalty (the smoothing parameter) estimated by REML, and `parsnip::gen_additive_mod()` is the book's `parsnip` face for it, with `mgcv` as the engine. I will show the pair on the adjusted model of the next section. The two agree in the way that the other pairs of this book agree: with a weakly informative prior on the smooth's standard deviation and 130 participants, the likelihood does most of the work, and the REML estimate of the penalty is close to the posterior of `sds`. They differ in the usual places. The `mgcv` band is a confidence band for the curve conditional on the estimated smoothing parameter, which does not carry the uncertainty about the smoothing parameter itself; the `brms` band does, and is a little wider.

When should you prefer a spline to the other two curves of @sec-longitudinal-timeseries? The mechanistic curve is the right choice when you have a *recipe*, because its parameters mean something (a rate, a plateau, a day of the peak) and it extrapolates by its own logic. The Gaussian process is the right choice when you want a smooth with a length-scale that you can interpret and a prior that reverts to the average where there are no data. The spline is the right choice when you need a *flexible nuisance or an exploratory shape*, which is most of the time, because it plugs into any formula, with any family, and with several smooths at once. A spline of a single variable and a Gaussian process with a squared-exponential covariance are close relatives, and in `mgcv` the Gaussian-process smooth is one of the available bases, as the last chapter showed. They are not rivals; they are different defaults.

## A curve as an adjustment: speech, age and sex {#sec-cis-pk}

Of all the jobs that I give a spline, the commonest is the humblest: it looks after a variable that I have to account for and that I do not want to force into a straight line. That is the second half of this chapter's promise, a diagram that tells me *which* variables to hold fixed and a curve that lets them be held fixed *as they are*. I will show it twice, with data in which I can say something about what the groups look like: the speech of people with Parkinson's disease, and the NeuN sections.

The Parkinson data are the ones of @sec-ordinal-nominal-regression [@hlavnicka2017; @hlavnicka2017uci]: 130 participants (50 healthy controls, 50 people with REM sleep behaviour disorder and 30 with early untreated Parkinson's disease), one reading task, and speech features computed from the recordings. In that chapter I chose two features with the data in view; I take the first of them, the **rate of speech timing** (how fast the syllables follow each other, per minute), and standardize it, so that the outcome is in standard deviations (one standard deviation is 47 per minute). @fig-cis_pk_age carries the two lessons. The first is about the curve. With 12 percentage points more women among the participants with PD than among the controls, and women speaking faster in this sample, the raw difference is pulled toward zero, and adjusting for sex and age moves it a little in the direction that the imbalance predicts (PD minus controls goes from -0.71 [-1.13, -0.27] to -0.77 [-1.15, -0.37] standard deviations; the first row against the second). But changing the age adjustment from a straight line to a smooth moves it by almost nothing: -0.77 [-1.15, -0.37] with the line and -0.75 [-1.15, -0.37] with the smooth. That is not a failure of the spline. It is what was to be expected from the diagram and the numbers: age is nearly independent of the group here, so *how* it enters the model can change little. The right habit is to check, and not to assume that a flexible adjustment always changes the answer. The second lesson is about the medication, in the last row: holding the benzodiazepine fixed moves the RBD-minus-control difference to -0.46 [-0.81, -0.12], against -0.39 [-0.73, -0.05] without it. That is the bad control of @tbl-cis_controls at work. The shift is small here because only 12 of the 80 patients take one, and I would not want you to take the small size as reassurance; the problem is in the logic, and no healthy control takes a benzodiazepine, so the model learns the effect of the drug from the patients alone, and "holding it fixed" asks for a comparison between patients and controls *with the same medication*, which does not exist.

**Frequentist equivalent.** The two agree in the way the single-level models of the book do: with weak priors and 130 participants, the likelihood does most of the work. The group differences of the least-squares fits are within a few hundredths of a standard deviation of the posterior medians, and the REML smooth has 1.9 effective degrees of freedom against a posterior curve that travels about as far. Where they part is in the bands (the REML band is conditional on the estimated smoothing parameter) and in what the prior does at the ends of the age axis, where there are few participants.

A paragraph about what this comparison *is*, because it is easy to read too much into it. These are 130 people in a research sample, and the groups are not random draws from any population: they were recruited. Even the adjusted difference is a statement about the people of this study, under a diagram that includes age and sex and nothing else, and it says nothing about what Parkinson's disease does to speech in a person, nor does it tell you whether a person has the disease, which is what the last section of @sec-ordinal-nominal-regression showed. A group difference of a standard deviation is compatible with a speech rate that is useless for classifying any individual. I report it as a feature of the sample, and the sentence for a paper below says so.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it: speech rate in Parkinson's disease"}
**Results.** In 130 participants (50 healthy controls, 50 with REM sleep behaviour disorder and 30 with early Parkinson's disease), the rate of speech timing in a reading task was 0.75 [0.37, 1.15] standard deviations lower in Parkinson's disease than in healthy controls (about 36 [17, 54] per minute fewer) and 0.39 [0.05, 0.73] standard deviations lower in REM sleep behaviour disorder (posterior medians and 95% credible intervals; posterior probability that the rate is lower, above 0.999 and 0.987), adjusted for sex and for age with a smooth. Women had higher rates than men by 0.82 [0.44, 1.18] standard deviations.

**Methods.** The adjustment set (age and sex) was chosen from a causal diagram in which the group may differ in sex and age and both affect speech; medication was not adjusted for, because it is a consequence of the diagnosis. The standardized rate was modeled with a Gaussian likelihood, group and sex as categories and age as a penalized smooth (six basis functions; Normal(0, 1) for the coefficients and Exponential(1) for the standard deviation of the smooth), in `brms` (four chains of 4,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 for all parameters). The groups were recruited and not assigned, so the differences are descriptive of this sample and are not evidence of an effect of the disease on speech.

## A diagram for what is missing {#sec-cis-missing}

At the end of @sec-missing-data-measurement-error I left a sentence hanging: that a diagram of what causes the loss is exactly what tells you whether the loss is ignorable. Here is that sentence, drawn. The idea is to add to the diagram a node for *being observed* (call it `Present`) and ask what points into it. If the arrows into `Present` come only from variables that are in the model, the missing values are [ignorable]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} given those variables: they are what @sec-eda-missing-data called missing at random, and a model that conditions on them is not misled. If an arrow comes from the value itself, or from a variable that also drives the value and is not in the model, they are not: that is missing not at random, and no formula can fix it [@mcelreath2020; @huntingtonklein2021]. The missingness mechanisms of the earlier chapter are three small causal diagrams, and this is the first time the book draws them.

The NeuN sections are the first case. Daniel's account of why the posterior sections go missing is anatomical: that part of the brain is more fragile, and sections of it are lost more often under the blade of the cryostat. That makes position a cause of whether a section exists. Position also changes the density (the cortex is not the same at every level; in the data of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts the right hemisphere gains about a third in density from the anterior end to the fifth section, as @fig-cis_neun shows below). The injury changes the density, and I draw a dashed arrow from the injury to whether a section is present, because four sections were lost *inside* the series of ischemic mice (@sec-missing-data-measurement-error). And I draw, in grey, the thing that nobody measured and that would change the answer: the condition of the tissue at the moment of cutting, which can both make a section break and lower the count of neurons.






::: {.cell}

The first statement says that, in the simple diagram, the density of a section is independent of whether the section was *present* once the position and the injury are known. That is the claim that justifies using every section that exists in the model, and it is the claim that a spline of position makes: the smooth is how the model holds the position fixed without forcing it to enter as a straight line. In the full diagram the answer is `FALSE`: the unmeasured tissue condition connects `Present` and `Density` through a path that neither position nor injury blocks. The assumption of ignorability is the assumption that this grey box does not exist, or does not matter, and a diagram cannot be argued with more clearly than that.

The diagram makes one prediction that the data *can* check. If the loss of the seventh section depends only on position, then mice that have a seventh section and mice that do not should have the same density in sections 1 to 6, at the same position, day and hemisphere. @sec-cis-neun shows that check, with the result.

The second diagram is the open-field one. There the tracker loses the mouse, and the lost sessions had little time in the center and were concentrated on day 1 (@sec-missing-data-measurement-error). I read that as the tracker losing the animal for something that the animal does, which also changes its time in the center: freezing or hugging a wall. That is an unmeasured variable with an arrow into both the outcome and the loss, and the graph is not repairable: there is nothing in the data to hold fixed. The honest response is the one of the earlier chapter, a tipping-point analysis that asks *how different would the lost sessions have to be* for the conclusion to change, and I do not repeat it. What the diagram adds is the reason that no clever model of the kept sessions can substitute for it.


## The sections of the cortex: a smooth for the position {#sec-cis-neun}

The second use of a spline as an adjustment comes with a promise that I made in @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts. There I added the position of the section as a factor, saw that the injury effects did not move, and wrote that this was not luck: both hemispheres of a section share its position, so a position effect cancels in the left-minus-right comparison. I left position out of the main model. That argument is correct, and it is a statement about a *within-section* comparison. It says nothing about the comparison *between mice*, which is where position can come back. A mouse that lost its seventh section has an average that is taken over six positions, and one that kept it over seven; if the density changes along the anterior-posterior axis, those two averages are not the same kind of number. The diagram of @fig-cis_miss_dags (left) says what makes position matter: it affects the density and it affects whether the section exists, and a model that holds the position fixed, without forcing the density to be a straight line in it, is the tool that the diagram asks for.













The model is the one of the multilevel chapters (a level for each mouse and for each section) with a smooth of the position added, one curve for each hemisphere, because the injury is not the same at every level of the brain. The smooth has five building blocks, a prior of `Exponential(3)` on its standard deviation (the log density varies by a few tenths along the axis, and the prior says so) and the priors of the earlier chapters for the rest. I fit it and the model without it, which is the model of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Priors of the multilevel chapters: log density around 6.7 (about 800 cells per mm2), a spread of the smooth
prior_neun <- c(prior(normal(6.7, 0.5), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
                prior(exponential(3), class = "sd"), prior(exponential(3), class = "sigma"))
prior_neun_s <- c(prior_neun, prior(exponential(3), class = "sds"))

# 12. Without the position of the section (the model of the multilevel chapters)
fit_n0 <- brm(log_dens ~ dpi * hemi + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section), data = cortex, prior = prior_neun,
              chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 3000, seed = 123, control = ctl, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/causal-inference-splines_fit12.rds", file_refit = "never")

              file = "models/causal-inference-splines_fit13.rds", file_refit = "never")

A smooth lets the two hemispheres each have the curve that they have, and the *difference* between the curves along the axis is information that a single coefficient for the injury would have hidden: the injury is not uniform from front to back.

I drew the left panel of @fig-cis_neun with `geom_ribbon()` and `geom_line()` over every section, with the density on a logarithmic axis, because the model is for the log density and equal distances on that axis are equal *ratios* of cells, which is how the injury effect is reported. The design tip is the one of @sec-longitudinal-timeseries: when a model has a smooth, draw it over the points that it was fit to, and let the band show where there are few of them.

The right panel is what the adjustment does to the effects that the chapter on varying intercepts was about. Both models give nearly the same left-minus-right differences, within a few hundredths on the log scale (and that is the cancellation, working as it should), and nearly the same between-mouse differences between days. The two comparisons that the smooth *could* have moved, the differences between days in the right hemisphere, move by less than 0.01 on the log scale (about one percent of the density), far less than the width of the intervals. So here is the honest summary: *the adjustment was right and it was not needed*. The diagram told me to hold position fixed; the data say that the missing sections are too few and too spread over the groups (@fig-cis_miss_dags again, and @sec-missing-data-measurement-error) to bias the day effects noticeably. I would not have known that without doing it.

**Frequentist equivalent.** `mgcv` with the mouse and the section written as random-effect smooths is the REML version of the same multilevel model, and its coefficients for the day, the hemisphere and their interactions are within a few hundredths of the posterior medians; the effective degrees of freedom of the two position smooths are 2.5 and 2 (1 would be a straight line). The only place where they would differ in a way that matters is the posterior end of the axis, where `brms` shows the uncertainty of the smooth and of its standard deviation together, and the REML band conditions on the estimated penalty.

The diagram also made a prediction that the data can check, and I said that I would. If the loss of the seventh section depends only on position, then the mice that have a seventh section and those that do not should have the same density in sections 1 to 6, given the position, the day and the hemisphere. The last NeuN fit adds a variable for *having a seventh section* (a mouse-level indicator) to the sections 1 to 6. Its coefficient is 0.02 [-0.11, 0.16] on the log scale: mice with a seventh section have a density that is, in the posterior median, 2% different from those without, with an interval that includes no difference. That is a *check*, not a proof: it can contradict the diagram (a large and clear coefficient would say that the lost sections are related to the tissue in a way that position does not explain), and it did not. What it cannot do is rule out that the tissue condition of the missing sections themselves, the ones nobody counted, is different.

## When the shape is the finding {#sec-cis-finding}

In both examples so far the curve was *looking after* a variable that I did not care about, and what I reported was the effect that the curve made it possible to estimate. There is another use of a spline, and the right way to use it is different: the curve *is* the result. A dose-response curve is the standard case. If I give a drug at six doses, the question is not "is there a slope?" but "does the effect rise and then flatten, is there a threshold below which nothing happens, does it turn down at the high doses?". The shape answers the question, and so the model, the prior and the reading all change. The questions that matter are where the curve changes, how steep it is at a given value, and how sure I am of each of those, and the right way to answer them is from the posterior of the curve, as in @sec-lt-derived.

I do not have a real dose-response in this book. The files that I use have no continuous dose or intensity of an intervention (a drug dose, a stimulation intensity, a measured lesion size), and I will not invent one: a chapter on dose-response needs data in which the dose was set by the experimenter. I leave the requirement written down for a later edition (**PENDING-DATA**: a real experiment with a continuous dose or intensity, preferably six or more levels, with the outcome per animal or per sample and the design stated).

The closest question in the data that I do have is the one that opened the chapter, and it can be asked as a question about shape. Within the animals that had an ischemia, with the day held fixed, **is the relationship of the tissue area to each marker straight, or does it bend?** A marker could do nothing up to some level and then protect the tissue, which a straight line would average away. @fig-cis_smooth_markers is the smooth of each marker, in a model that also holds the day fixed (as a category) and the other marker at its mean, and lets the spread differ by day as in the rest of the chapter. The days themselves do not get a spline: with five distinct days, a smooth of the day is a Gaussian process or a mechanistic curve in disguise, and @sec-longitudinal-timeseries is where that was done properly.






::: {.cell}

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read a smooth in this order. First the *band*, not the line: where is it narrow and where wide? It is wide where there are few animals, and that is where the line has no authority. Second, ask whether a *straight line* would fit inside the band from end to end; if it does, the curve has not shown any bend. Third, look at the middle, where the animals are, and ask how much the curve travels compared with the vertical scatter of the points. The mistake to avoid is to read the wiggles at the ends: the last stretch of a smooth is determined by a few animals and by the prior, and a wiggle there is the penalty making up its mind.
:::













The answer is that the curves are close to straight lines. In @fig-cis_smooth_markers the median curve of GFAP rises by 1.3 mm² across the range of the animals, with a band that holds a horizontal line from one end to the other; the one of PDGFR-β falls by 2.4 mm², with a band that only just holds one. ## Where the diagram can be wrong {#sec-cis-limits}

Everything in this chapter depends on the diagrams, and the diagrams are mine. I want to say clearly what that does and does not allow. A diagram is a **claim**, not a result. The data can contradict some claims and cannot confirm any: a graph tells you which *statistical* statements it implies (which variables should be independent of which, given others), and you can test those implications, but a graph that passes the tests has only survived, and a different graph might have survived too.

Both halves of that sentence can be shown with the data of this chapter. For the first half, the ischemia diagram without the lesion size says that the two markers are independent of each other once the group is known (the fork of @fig-cis_three_dags); the data have a say, if a quiet one.

### A sensitivity statement, not a cure {#sec-cis-sensitivity-rv}

If the adjustment set of a diagram is "everything that matters, observed", what remains is the thing that is not observed, and the useful question is not "is there an unmeasured confounder?" (there always is) but **how strong would it have to be to change my conclusion?** Cinelli and Hazlett [@cinelli2020] gave a simple answer in the units of a linear model: the *robustness value* is the share of the residual variance of both the exposure and the outcome that an unmeasured variable would have to explain, *at the same time*, to reduce the estimated effect to zero. A confounder that explains less than that of either cannot do it. The same logic works with risk ratios (the E-value of @ding2016), which is the better tool for a binary outcome.

The place where this matters in this chapter is the Parkinson comparison, because it is observational. The total effect on the tissue area is protected by the randomization, and the sensitivity of the direct effect is already settled (it is not identified). For the speech comparison, the quantity is the difference in the rate of speech timing between participants with PD and healthy controls, adjusted for age and sex, in a linear model that I fit by least squares to use the formula.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The linear model of the adjustment set, by least squares (the frequentist counterpart of fit 7)
lm_pk <- lm(z_rate ~ group + sex + age10, data = pk)

# Robustness value of Cinelli and Hazlett, by hand: the partial Cohen's f of the PD coefficient, then the value
# (checked against the sensemakr package on a simulated example, where both give the same numbers)
rv_fun <- function(model, term, q = 1, alpha = NULL) {
  tt <- summary(model)$coefficients[term, "t value"]; dof <- model$df.residual
  f <- q * abs(tt) / sqrt(dof)
  if (!is.null(alpha)) f <- f - qt(1 - alpha / 2, dof - 1) / sqrt(dof - 1)
  0.5 * (sqrt(f^4 + 4 * f^2) - f^2)
}
rv_pd <- rv_fun(lm_pk, "groupPD")
rv_pd_a <- rv_fun(lm_pk, "groupPD", alpha = 0.05)
rv_rbd <- rv_fun(lm_pk, "groupRBD")
rv_rbd_a <- rv_fun(lm_pk, "groupRBD", alpha = 0.05)

# For context: the partial R2 of the strongest measured covariate (sex) with the outcome
tt_sex <- summary(lm_pk)$coefficients["sexF", "t value"]
r2_sex <- tt_sex^2 / (tt_sex^2 + lm_pk$df.residual)
```
:::






For PD against healthy controls, the robustness value is 30%: an unmeasured variable that explained 30% of the remaining variance both of the group and of the speech rate (and nothing else) would be enough to bring the estimated difference to zero, and 16% would be enough to make the interval include zero. For RBD against controls the values are 19% and 3%. To put that in proportion: sex, the strongest variable that I did measure, explains 13% of the remaining variance of the speech rate. So the question for the reader is whether an unmeasured variable could be *more* strongly related to speech than sex is, and also more strongly related to being a patient. That is a judgment about the study (the recruitment, the education, the dialect of the participants, the severity), and the statement is a way of saying what the judgment is about. I did not choose the numbers to rescue the result; they are what the formula gives.

The left panel is the good case: the simulated speech rates surround the observed ones. The right panel is not, and I would rather show it than hide it. The observed densities of the NeuN data have a sharp peak and stop near 7 on the log scale, with a long tail toward low values, and a Gaussian model produces symmetric, wider humps that extend past that edge. This is the misfit that @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts found and handled with a Student-*t* likelihood, and it is not what this chapter is about: the smooth of position and the coefficients that I compared do not depend on it, and I kept the Gaussian model so that the only thing that changes between the two NeuN fits is the smooth. But a reader who wants to *use* the position curve for prediction would have to fix the likelihood first.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Compare the dark line with the cloud of light ones. If the light lines surround the dark one and have the same hump, the model can reproduce the shape of the outcome. If the dark line leaves the cloud (a second hump, a longer tail, a cliff at a boundary), the model is missing a feature. This check looks at the *whole* outcome; it does not say that the smooth has the right shape at every age, which is why the figure of the curve and its band is the other half of the check. The mistake to avoid is reading a good overlap as proof that the diagram is right: the check tests the *distribution of the outcome*, not the arrows.
:::

## What the chapter settled, and where Part 5 ends {#sec-cis-close}

We started with a marker that moved with the tissue loss and a coefficient that I could not interpret, and I hope you take away a habit more than a method. **Draw the diagram before you choose the covariates**, and look every covariate up in it: a variable that causes both exposure and outcome belongs in the model; a variable on the way from one to the other does not, if you want the total effect; a variable that two causes meet in does not, whatever the correlation looks like, and neither does selecting the rows by it. A diagram is a **claim**: the randomization in the ischemia experiment protected the total effect, and the same diagram showed that the "direct effect" through the markers cannot be estimated honestly with the variables I have. The coefficients of the covariates of an adjusted model are not their effects, and I do not report them. And a standardized difference, the average predictive comparison that you have been computing since @sec-logistic-regression, is a causal effect only to the extent that the diagram says so.

The second habit is about curves. A spline is a regression with synthetic predictors and a penalty, and the penalty (the standard deviation of the weights, or the smoothing parameter of `mgcv`) is what lets you start with more building blocks than you need. Read it by its band before its line, and say what a straight line would have to do to fit inside it. Use it as an *adjustment* to let a nuisance variable be as curved as the world is, and check, as I did twice, whether the curve moved anything; use it as the *finding* only when the shape is the question, and say, as the last section did, when the answer is "it does not bend". Neither the diagram nor the curve is a result by itself. They are what makes a result mean what you say it means, and both can be argued with, which is the point.

Part 5 is finished with this chapter, and it is worth saying what it did. It began with rows that are not evidence, because cells live in sections that live in mice ([the opener of the part](multilevel-intro.qmd#sec-multilevel-intro) and @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts), gave each animal its own response (@sec-multilevel-varying-slopes) and brought the families back with levels (@sec-multilevel-glmm). It graded neurological deficit in categories (@sec-ordinal-nominal-regression) and modeled the spread as well as the mean (@sec-multivariate-distributional-regression). It followed the scar over thirty days (@sec-longitudinal-timeseries), dealt with the values that the microscope could not see (@sec-missing-data-measurement-error) and, in this chapter, asked what causes what and drew curves. The thread through all of them was the one the first chapter of the part promised: **a row is not a piece of evidence, and what a model assumes about where the rows come from is part of the model.**

Part 6 changes the question once more. The cells of the sections that we counted have *places*: an astrocyte is next to another astrocyte, and the GFAP-positive cells that I called a barrier in this chapter enclose the PDGFR-β cells in the center of the lesion. A barrier is a statement about geometry, and the independence problem of @sec-linear-regression-assumptions reappears in a new form, because cells that sit close together resemble each other in the way attempts of one mouse do. The next part, [Reading the geometry of tissue](spatial-intro.qmd), is about describing that geometry and testing statements about it. Two things from this chapter come with us: a diagram is a claim that someone has to be able to argue with, and a curve is only as good as the band that you read it with.
